title: POC weekly sync - throughput optimization
customer_attendees: Rajat Singh - Head of ML Eng
summary: Weekly POC sync to review throughput test results, discuss continuous batching and concurrency targets, debug an intermittent latency spike, and align on next steps: run two extra benchmark configs, share logs, and schedule a dedicated perf run with NVLink toggles. Decision leaning to tune queue depth + prefer dedicated nodes for steady-state production.
next_steps: Redwood to share detailed benchmark spreadsheet and run configs by 2026-06-25
Mercury Labs to run two additional throughput jobs (batch=128/256) and upload logs by 2026-06-30
Schedule 2-hour dedicated perf run with NVLink toggles the week of 2026-07-06
action_items: Jordan: export full flamegraph and GPU utilization timeline from today's run - due 2026-06-25
Sofia: collect container logs and kernel dmesg from failing pod and upload to shared bucket - due 2026-06-26
Maya: send pricing note for dedicated nodes and pilot contract template - due 2026-06-26
transcript:
Header: 2026-06-24 16:00 UTC | Duration: ~45m | Attendees: Maya (Redwood AE), Jordan (Redwood SE), Luis (Redwood Perf), Rajat (Mercury Head ML), Sofia (Mercury Platform), Ethan (CTO)

00:00 Maya: hey everyone thanks for joining, can you hear me ok?
00:04 Rajat: yeah loud and clear, thanks Maya.
00:08 Maya: cool, quick agenda — recap last week's runs, results Luigi? sorry Luis — throughput numbers, discuss continuous batching tuning, concurrency targets, queueing/backpressure, open issues, next steps. anything to add?
00:20 Rajat: no that's it. main thing is the intermittent p95 spike we've been seeing — want to understand root cause.

01:02 Jordan: ok jump in on the results. so we ran three main configs: hosted fastpath (shared pool), dedicated 4xA100, and an experimental batcher with continuous batching enabled. the best steady throughput was on dedicated with batching enabled: ~14k tokens/sec for our 512-token workload, p95 around 210ms most of the time.
01:36 Sofia: that's better than last week, but we saw several 800-1,200ms p95 spikes, usually around minute 12 and 27 in the run.
01:45 Luis: yep those align with a recompile/GC-ish blip; we dug into GPU metrics and saw a brief drop in GPU concurrency plus a host OOM on one node in one run. logs attached.
02:05 Rajat: host OOM? we didn't expect memory pressure — we thought model footprint was stable. what caused OOM?
02:13 Luis: looks like under peak queue depth we had slightly larger KV cache retention coupled with our larger batch size; the host had other processes from earlier tests; container-level mem limit was hit then the node started thrashing.
02:28 Ethan: are these logs the ones we uploaded to the shared sheet? i saw an entry flagged at 16:12 UTC.
02:35 Jordan: yes that's the one. link to spreadsheet in the chat (https://redwood-internal/benchmarks/mercury-2026-06-24). note the sheet has the run ids.

03:10 Maya: ok on continuous batching — quick recap for the team: continuous batching lets the runtime aggregate incoming requests into a rolling batch, which increases GPU utilization and amortizes KV cache overhead, but it adds a queueing delay. we were aiming for sub-200ms p95, is that still the target?
03:28 Rajat: yes sub-200 p95 ideally, but we can compromise to 300ms for the peak if throughput gains are huge. the product team wants 10k tokens/sec sustained at 95% uptime.
03:39 Luis: based on today's runs, to hit 10k steady we need to target concurrency of ~36 workers with batch size ~192-256 and queue depth tuning to avoid OOMs. continuous batching at those params gave best efficiency.
03:56 Sofia: how do we reason about queue depth? we've seen latency tail because queue grows under bursty traffic.
04:03 Jordan: good question. queue depth is basically how many inflight requests the system will hold to assemble batches. too shallow and you starve the GPU leading to lower throughput; too deep and you add tail latency and expose memory pressure. we recommend a dynamic queue that scales with measured arrival rate and an upper soft cap tied to mem headroom.

05:10 Rajat: is that implemented in the POC runtime or do we need the Redwood team to patch?
05:15 Luis: current POC has a basic dynamic queue but we can push a policy tweak: soft cap at 200 requests, hard cap at 320, and evict the oldest low-priority requests when we approach memory thresholds. we'll test with those numbers.
05:30 Ethan: what about prefetch / KV cache warms? are cache misses causing spikes?
05:35 Jordan: some of them — when we scale concurrency up quickly KV cache gets fragmented and cold entries cause extra decoding cost. continuous batching helps because it maintains KV affinity per session. also we suggested sticky routing for sessions during the POC to keep KV locality.
05:52 Rajat: sticky routing seemed to help last week. are we recommending sticky for prod?
05:56 Luis: yes for stateful session workloads. it slightly reduces overall throughput in extreme multi-tenant shared pools, but for Mercury's workload of long sessions it's a net win.

07:10 Sofia: there was also a note about model variant fallback in the run where a node flaked — we saw automatic fallback but latency jumped — can we tune fallbacks?
07:19 Jordan: fallback is currently immediate to a smaller quantized variant; we can add a grace period and try retry-on-same-node for short blips, or fallback with a warm cache overlay. that's an engineering change but doable for pilot.
07:35 Maya: ok good.

08:00 Rajat: about concurrency targets — you mentioned 36 workers. can you map that to our deployment size? how many GPUs/nodes?
08:09 Luis: with our 4xA100 cluster we used 8 workers per GPU (approx) to keep per-worker mem low; so 36 workers maps to 4-5 GPUs. with dedicated nodes we'd provision 4 GPUs and reserve one spare for failing-over. that aligns with the dedicated config we tested.
08:28 Ethan: for budgeting, is dedicated required or can we hit targets on hosted?
08:34 Jordan: hosted shared pools can hit targets but cost variability and noisy neighbors cause the p95 spikes. for predictable SLOs Redwood recommends dedicated pools for steady state at scale. we can provide cost vs latency curves in the spreadsheet.

09:10 Sofia: on the intermittent 800-1200ms spikes, are we confident those are host OOMs vs driver issue?
09:18 Luis: from kernel logs it's host OOM plus a brief NVML driver reset in one case. likely memory pressure cascaded into kernel-level behaviour. the fix path: reduce per-request mem by lowering batch max and improve the queue eviction policy; also set container memory reservation.
09:36 Rajat: can you quantify the throughput delta if we set batch to 128 instead of 256?
09:42 Jordan: approximate: batch=256 gave 14k tokens/sec, batch=128 gives ~11k tokens/sec but reduces mem by ~30% and lowers tail risk. batch=192 is a compromise at ~12.8k. we'll validate in the next runs.

11:00 Maya: Luis, what about continuous batching latency breakdown — can you walk through the flamegraph?
11:05 Luis: sure. attaching quick take: time is mostly token generation on GPU (80%), small section (8%) waiting for batch assembly, and ~12% I/O/serialization. spikes show an extra 150-400ms spent in kernel context switches and page faults during OOM.
11:22 Sofia: page faults — is that swap? we don't want swap.
11:25 Luis: right, those are file-backed page faults from host-level memory reclaim; disabling swap and pinning mem prevents that; we recommended docker runtime flags in the doc.

12:00 Rajat: great — so immediate action: run batch sizes 128 and 192 with queue caps 200/320 and collect full GPU traces. Sofia will upload logs.
12:09 Sofia: yes, we'll run those tonight and upload.
12:12 Jordan: we'll also run an extra experiment with NVLink disabled vs enabled in the dedicated run so we can measure cross-GPU communication costs; schedule a 2-hour dedicated window next week.

13:05 Ethan: what about SLO release criteria — if we hit 10k tokens/sec p95<300ms for 30m window is that acceptable?
13:12 Maya: sounds reasonable as an interim target. final production bar we'll lock after a longer soak and error-rate review.

13:40 Rajat: any security or compliance blockers in dedicated? we need KMS integration and audit logs.
13:45 Jordan: Redwood Private supports KMS/HSM and audit logging; for the demo/pilot we have S3-compatible audit exports turned on and we'll share SOC2 artifacts. Maya will follow up.
13:58 Maya: noted — I'll send the security pack with SOC2 and network diagram.

15:10 Sofia: small thing — can Redwood instrument request-level queue latency in the console? it'd help us tune in near real-time.
15:16 Jordan: yes that's on Redwood Console roadmap; we can expose a per-route queue histogram for the pilot by next week as a feature flag.
15:25 Maya: ok Jordan to enable that for Mercury.

16:00 Maya: any other open questions?
16:03 Rajat: just one — do you have guidance on autoscaling thresholds for throughput vs latency?
16:10 Luis: general guideline: scale up when throughput plateaus for N=3 consecutive intervals and p95 > target, scale down when underutilized for 5 minutes; tie to GPU utilization (%80+) and queue growth. we will provide a config template.
16:28 Rajat: excellent.

17:00 Maya: recap of next steps: Redwood to share benchmark spreadsheet and run configs (Jordan), Redwood to push the queue policy tweak to the POC branch (Luis), Mercury to run batch=128/192 with caps and upload logs (Sofia), schedule dedicated perf window week of 7/6 (all). pricing note for dedicated pilot from Maya.
17:22 Ethan: thanks team.
17:25 Maya: thanks everyone, we'll follow up in email and drop the sheet link. talk soon.

End transcript.
